rows.title: Zameldowanie — address registration at municipality
rows.description: Zameldowanie (address registration) is the mandatory registration of one's place of residence with the local municipality (gmina/urząd gminy). Poland distinguishes between permanent registration (zameldowanie na pobyt stały) and temporary registration (zameldowanie na pobyt czasowy — for stays over 3 months). For EU/EEA citizens and non-EU citizens with a valid residence title, registration is required within 30 days of arriving at a new address. Registration is done in person at the local Urząd Gminy or Urząd Miasta, at the Wydział Ewidencji Ludności (Population Registry). Documents required: valid passport or EU identity card, document confirming right to occupy the premises (rental contract, property deed, or written consent of the landlord/property owner). The landlord or property owner must confirm the registration on the form (potwierdzenie pobytu). There is no fee. Online registration (ePUAP/gov.pl) is available for those with a Profil Zaufany or e-ID. Zameldowanie is important: it triggers PESEL issuance for EU citizens staying over 3 months, and is required to access many local services.
required_documents: valid passport or EU identity card
rental contract or property ownership document
landlord/property owner confirmation on registration form
for non-EU: valid Karta Pobytu, work visa, or other residence title
rows.where_to_go: Urząd Gminy or Urząd Miasta — Wydział Ewidencji Ludności (Population Registry); or online via gov.pl (ePUAP) with Profil Zaufany
rows.notes: Both permanent and temporary registration is possible. Temporary registration (pobyt czasowy) is for stays expected to exceed 3 months but not permanent. Zameldowanie does NOT grant any residency rights to non-EU nationals — it is a purely administrative procedure confirming your address.
rows.source_quote: Zameldowanie stałe, zameldowanie czasowe, wymeldowanie — all persons residing in Poland must register their address with the local municipality.

rows.title: Apply for Karta Pobytu (residence card) — non-EU nationals only
rows.description: The Karta Pobytu (residence card) is the official residence document for non-EU nationals legally residing in Poland. It is required for extended stays beyond the initial visa validity. Applications are submitted to the Urząd Wojewódzki (Regional Governor's Office — Voivodeship Office) in the region where the applicant resides. As of April 27, 2026, applications must be submitted exclusively through the MOS (Moduł Obsługi Spraw) online portal. The application must generally be filed before the current permission to stay expires. Processing times vary significantly by region and type of permit — typically 3–12 months; an application receipt (zaświadczenie) is issued which serves as proof of legal stay during processing. Types include: temporary residence (pobyt czasowy — typically 1–3 years, for work, study, family reunification), permanent residence (pobyt stały — after 5 years of continuous legal stay), and EU long-term residence permit. Supporting documents vary by permit type but typically include: valid passport, proof of accommodation, employment contract or employer's letter, proof of sufficient financial resources, and residence registration (zameldowanie). Fee: approx. 340–440 PLN (~€80–100) depending on permit type.
required_documents: valid entry visa or prior residence document
proof of accommodation (rental contract or zameldowanie)
rows.where_to_go: MOS online portal (mos.gov.pl) for submission; then Urząd Wojewódzki (Voivodeship Office) for biometrics and document collection
rows.notes: Since April 27, 2026, applications must be submitted exclusively via the MOS system. The application receipt (zaświadczenie o złożeniu wniosku) allows the applicant to remain legally in Poland while the application is being processed. Processing can take 6–12 months in busy regions (Warsaw). Start early.
rows.source_name: Urząd do Spraw Cudzoziemców (Office for Foreigners) — gov.pl/udsc
rows.source_quote: Od 27 kwietnia 2026r. składanie wniosków o pobyt w Polsce wyłącznie przez MOS. [From April 27, 2026, applications for residence in Poland must be submitted exclusively through MOS.]

rows.title: NIP (tax identification number) — automatic upon PESEL registration
rows.description: The NIP (Numer Identyfikacji Podatkowej — Tax Identification Number) is Poland's tax ID number. For individuals who are not VAT-registered sole traders, the PESEL number functions as the personal tax identifier — so employees do not typically need a separate NIP. When an employee registers with PESEL and begins employment, the employer uses the PESEL number for all tax reporting (PIT declarations, payslips). The employer deducts income tax (PIT) and health insurance contributions from salary and remits them to the tax authority (Urząd Skarbowy). At year end, the employer issues a PIT-11 form summarizing the employee's income and tax withheld. Employees should submit or verify their annual PIT return (usually PIT-37 for employees) by April 30 of the following year, available online at e-Urząd Skarbowy (podatki.gov.pl). Foreign employees on Polish employment contracts are typically Polish tax residents if spending more than 183 days/year in Poland.
required_documents: PESEL number (employer uses this for tax reporting)
PIT-2 form (submitted to employer to declare tax-free amount)
rows.where_to_go: Employer handles tax registration and deduction; employee files annual return online at podatki.gov.pl (e-Urząd Skarbowy) or at local Urząd Skarbowy
rows.notes: Employees should submit PIT-2 form to employer to claim the annual tax-free allowance (kwota zmniejszająca podatek). Annual PIT-37 filing deadline is April 30. Tax office pre-fills returns using employer data — accessible at podatki.gov.pl with Profil Zaufany or mObywatel.
rows.source_quote: For individuals, the PESEL number serves as the tax identifier (NIP) for income tax purposes; employers use the PESEL for all PIT reporting obligations.

rows.title: NFZ health insurance enrollment — access to Polish public healthcare
rows.description: The NFZ (Narodowy Fundusz Zdrowia — National Health Fund) is Poland's public health insurance system. All employees working under an employment contract (umowa o pracę) are automatically enrolled in NFZ by their employer as part of ZUS registration — health insurance contributions (składka zdrowotna, 9% of gross minus social security contributions) are deducted by the employer. Coverage extends to the employee's family members (spouse, children) who are not independently insured. Upon enrollment, the employee is entitled to use public healthcare services (POZ — Primary Care, specialist care, hospital treatment) covered by NFZ. To access healthcare: present your PESEL number and identity document — the eWUŚ system electronically verifies insurance status in real time at any NFZ-contracted facility. To select a primary care physician (lekarz POZ — Podstawowa Opieka Zdrowotna), submit a declaration form at the chosen clinic. For voluntary insurance (self-employed, students), apply directly at the local NFZ branch with a ZUS ZKW form.
required_documents: PESEL number (employer registers on behalf of employee)
for family members: birth certificates and marriage certificate if applicable
rows.where_to_go: Employer handles mandatory enrollment via ZUS; employee selects a primary care physician at a local POZ clinic; voluntary enrollment at NFZ branch office
rows.notes: eWUŚ electronic verification means you don't need to carry a physical insurance card — just PESEL and ID. For voluntary enrollment (e.g., for unemployed spouse), contact the local NFZ branch. The 'red' (czerwony) status in eWUŚ may appear during processing — employee can self-declare insurance in writing at the facility.

rows.title: ZUS social security registration (employer-led; employee monitors RMUA)
rows.description: ZUS (Zakład Ubezpieczeń Społecznych — Social Insurance Institution) is Poland's social security institution, covering pensions, disability, sickness, and accident insurance. For employees under an employment contract (umowa o pracę), the employer is legally required to register the employee with ZUS within 7 days of the employment start date (using form ZUS ZUA). The employer deducts employee contributions from gross salary and adds employer contributions. Employee contribution rates: pension (emerytalne) 9.76%, disability (rentowe) 1.5%, sickness (chorobowe) 2.45% — total approx. 13.71% of gross salary. Health insurance (NFZ) 9% (not ZUS but collected together). The employer provides a monthly RMUA (Raport Miesięczny Ubezpieczonego Osoby Ubezpieczonej lub Płatnika) statement — formerly a paper document, now accessible electronically via PUE ZUS portal. Employees can view their ZUS account, contribution history, and pension projections online at PUE ZUS (pue.zus.pl) using PESEL and a Profil Zaufany or ZUS account.
required_documents: PESEL number (employer registers employee using this)
rows.where_to_go: Employer handles registration; employee accesses ZUS account at pue.zus.pl
rows.notes: Employer must register within 7 days of employment start. Employee should verify that the first payslip shows ZUS contributions correctly split. PUE ZUS portal allows checking contribution history. ZUS contributions build up pension entitlements — important for those planning long-term residence.
rows.source_quote: The employer must register an employee with ZUS within 7 days of the commencement of employment using form ZUS ZUA.

rows.title: Open a Polish bank account
rows.description: A Polish bank account (konto osobiste) is needed to receive salary, pay rent, and manage daily finances. Most employers require a Polish bank account for salary payments. Major banks operating in Poland: PKO Bank Polski (largest Polish bank, extensive branch network), mBank (strong online banking, English-language interface), Santander Bank Polska (good English support), ING Bank Śląski (popular with expats). For non-EU nationals, PESEL is typically required by Polish banks; some banks may allow account opening with just a passport and residence permit before PESEL is obtained. For EU citizens: passport or EU identity card is usually sufficient. Online banks (Revolut, Wise, N26) can serve as a bridge before obtaining a PESEL. mBank and ING offer notably strong English-language online banking. Account opening can often be done fully online for EU citizens; non-EU nationals typically need an in-person branch visit.

PESEL number (required by most Polish banks)

rows.title: Driver's license — validity and conversion rules in Poland
rows.description: EU/EEA driving licenses are fully valid in Poland without any conversion requirement and remain valid for their original expiry date. When an EU license expires while the holder is resident in Poland, it must be exchanged for a Polish license at the Wydział Komunikacji (Transport Department) of the local Starostwo Powiatowe (County Office). Non-EU driving licenses are valid in Poland for a period defined by Polish law — generally for the duration of the holder's legal stay. Poland has bilateral exchange agreements with several countries; for others, the holder must pass the Polish theory test (egzamin z teorii) and practical test (egzamin z jazdy). The process for non-EU license conversion: apply at the Wydział Komunikacji with required documents, pass the applicable tests (if no bilateral agreement), obtain a Polish license. Poland is a signatory to the Vienna Convention on Road Traffic, which recognizes International Driving Permits (IDP).
required_documents: valid identity document (passport or EU ID)
medical fitness certificate (orzeczenie lekarskie) if required
rows.where_to_go: Wydział Komunikacji at local Starostwo Powiatowe (County Office) for license exchange; WORD (Wojewódzki Ośrodek Ruchu Drogowego) for theory and practical tests
rows.notes: EU license holders: no conversion needed during validity. Non-EU: check bilateral agreement status with local Wydział Komunikacji. IDP recommended for non-EU holders in the first year. Polish license exchange fee is approx. 100–200 PLN (€25–50).

rows.title: Enroll children in Polish school (szkoła podstawowa) or international school
rows.description: Compulsory education in Poland applies to children aged 7–18. Children of all nationalities residing in Poland have the right to public school education on equal terms with Polish children. Enrollment at a local state primary school (szkoła podstawowa) or secondary school is done by contacting the school directly or through the local gmina's school assignment system. Documents required: child's birth certificate (with certified Polish translation if foreign), vaccination records (karta szczepień), proof of address (zameldowanie or rental contract), and parent's/guardian's identity document and PESEL. For non-Polish-speaking children, state schools are required to provide Polish language support classes. In major cities, international schools are widely available: Warsaw International School (WIS), American School of Warsaw, British School Warsaw, International School of Krakow, and others — these have their own enrollment processes, fees (€5,000–€25,000/year), and waitlists. The school year runs September to June; mid-year enrollment is possible at any time.
required_documents: child's birth certificate (with certified Polish translation if foreign)
rows.where_to_go: Local szkoła podstawowa (primary school) or high school directly; local gmina's Wydział Edukacji for school assignments; international school admissions offices in Warsaw/Krakow/Wrocław/Gdańsk
rows.notes: State schools are free. For non-Polish-speaking children, the school must provide 'nauczanie języka polskiego' (Polish language teaching) as additional support per the Minister of Education's regulation. International schools require significant fees and early registration — waitlists can be 6–12 months in Warsaw.
rows.source_quote: Children of foreign nationals residing in Poland have the right to attend public schools on the same terms as Polish citizens.

rows.title: Obtain a Polish SIM card
rows.description: A Polish SIM card is needed for local communications, two-factor authentication for banking and government services, and to receive Polish administrative SMS notifications. Under Polish law implementing the EU Electronic Communications Code, SIM card registration requires identity verification. Required documents: valid passport or EU identity card; PESEL is not strictly required for prepaid SIM purchase but may be required for postpaid contracts. Major operators: Play, Orange Polska, T-Mobile Polska, Plus (Polkomtel). MVNOs: Virgin Mobile Polska, Lycamobile, Lebara. Prepaid (pre-paid/na kartę) SIMs are widely available at operator stores, Empik, Carrefour, Żabka, petrol stations, and electronics stores. Budget plans start from ~30–50 PLN/month (~€7–12) for unlimited calls and 15+ GB data. eSIM is available from Play and Orange for compatible devices.
required_documents: valid passport or EU identity card
PESEL (required for postpaid contracts; recommended for prepaid registration)
rows.where_to_go: Operator stores (Play, Orange, T-Mobile, Plus); supermarkets (Carrefour, Auchan); Empik; Żabka; petrol stations; online for eSIM (Play, Orange)
rows.notes: Prepaid SIMs do not require PESEL but must be registered with a valid ID per the Ustawa Prawo telekomunikacyjne. Play and Orange offer eSIM for compatible phones. Number portability (przeniesienie numeru) is possible — takes 1 working day.
rows.source_name: UKE — Urząd Komunikacji Elektronicznej (Office of Electronic Communications)
rows.source_quote: Operators are required to verify the identity of all SIM card purchasers under the Ustawa Prawo telekomunikacyjne, implementing EU Electronic Communications Code requirements.

sources: uke.gov.pl (T1 regulator — identity verification requirement confirmed)
Ustawa Prawo telekomunikacyjne (T1 legislative)

rows.title: Set up mObywatel app — Poland's digital identity platform
rows.description: mObywatel is Poland's official free government application that provides digital versions of key documents and enables online access to government services. The app is available on iOS (App Store) and Android (Google Play) and also accessible via browser at mObywatel.gov.pl. Key features include: mDowód (digital Polish identity card — legally accepted at offices, medical clinics, hotels, car rentals, and pharmacies), student ID (mLegitymacja), vehicle registration and driving history, qualified digital signatures (recognized across the EU), submission of electronic forms and applications to public authorities, and access to an official email inbox for government correspondence. To set up the app the user needs a valid Polish ID card or passport with NFC chip, and a PESEL number. A Profil Zaufany (trusted profile — Poland's electronic identity verification system) is recommended as it is required for many online gov.pl services and can be created through the mObywatel app itself.
required_documents: valid Polish ID card (dowód osobisty) or biometric passport with NFC chip
rows.where_to_go: Download from App Store or Google Play; or use browser at mObywatel.gov.pl; Profil Zaufany can be created online or at any public administration office (Urząd Gminy)
rows.notes: Non-EU nationals with Karta Pobytu can use mObywatel with their residence card as the identity document. The mDowód (digital ID) is legally equivalent to the physical ID card for most purposes. Profil Zaufany created through mObywatel enables pre-filled tax returns, ZUS access, and all gov.pl e-services.
rows.source_quote: mObywatel to: dziesiątki cyfrowych dokumentów, elektroniczne formularze i wnioski. [mObywatel is: dozens of digital documents, electronic forms and applications.]

sources: gov.pl/web/mobywatel (T1 — direct fetch, verbatim quote confirmed)

rows.title: Collect Employment Pass (EP) card and register fingerprints/photo
rows.description: After arriving in Singapore with your In-Principle Approval (IPA) letter, your employer must log in to EP eService to get the pass issued. If the notification letter states that biometrics registration is required, the candidate must make an appointment to register fingerprints and photo at ICA. The EP card is then delivered to the address provided within 5 working days after registration or document verification. The notification letter is valid for 1 month from issue and allows the candidate to start work while waiting for the card. Always carry your EP card as your primary identity document in Singapore.
required_documents: short-term visit pass or immigration pass details
rows.where_to_go: EP eService (mom.gov.sg) for employer; ICA appointment for biometrics if required; card delivered by post
rows.notes: Employer pays $225 pass issuance fee. Card arrives within 5 working days post-biometrics. The notification letter acts as interim authorisation to work and travel. Confirm with your employer whether biometrics are required — not all EP holders need this step.
rows.source_quote: Receive within 5 working days after fingerprint and photo registration, or document verification

rows.title: Understand your FIN (Foreign Identification Number)
rows.description: Your Foreign Identification Number (FIN) is printed on your EP card and begins with 'G' or 'M'. It is Singapore's equivalent of a national ID number for foreigners and is used for all government transactions including tax filing, CPF matters, SingPass registration, bank account opening, school enrollment, and healthcare. You do not need to separately apply for a FIN — it is automatically assigned when your work pass is issued. Memorise or securely record your FIN as it is required for almost every official interaction in Singapore.
rows.where_to_go: No action required — FIN is assigned automatically with the EP/S Pass
rows.notes: FIN also appears on the IPA letter before the physical card is issued. Used across IRAS, CPF, SingPass, ICA, MOE, and banking. S Pass holders also receive a FIN. LTVP holders receive their own FIN on their LTVP card.
rows.source_quote: Singapore Citizen, Permanent Resident or Foreign Identification Number (FIN) holder

rows.title: Register for SingPass account (Singapore's digital identity)
rows.description: SingPass is Singapore's national digital identity platform used to access over 2,000 government and private digital services. EP and S Pass holders with a valid FIN are eligible to register. Registration is done online at singpass.gov.sg — you will need your FIN, date of birth, and address as on your FIN card. The process uses Singpass Face Verification to verify identity instantly. After registration, download the Singpass app (iOS/Android), which replaces SMS-based two-factor authentication and allows QR-code login to government services. SingPass is essential for filing taxes (myTax Portal), ICA applications, CPF online access, and most government eServices.
required_documents: FIN (from EP card or IPA letter)
rows.where_to_go: Online at singpass.gov.sg — Face Verification available instantly; in-person help at SingPass counter (e.g. ICA Building or community centres) if online fails
rows.notes: FIN holders must ensure their address with ICA/MOM is correct before registering, as SingPass cross-checks address. SingPass app replaces SMS OTP. Face Verification works via smartphone camera. Non-IC holders (i.e. EP holders) follow the Foreign User Account (SFA) flow for some services.
rows.source_quote: You are a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident or Foreign Identification Number (FIN) holder

rows.title: Open a local bank account (DBS, OCBC, UOB or other)
rows.description: Opening a Singapore bank account is essential for receiving salary and managing local expenses. Major banks include DBS (DBS Multiplier account), OCBC (360 account), UOB, Citibank Singapore, and HSBC Singapore. Foreign EP holders can open an account in-branch or online. DBS allows foreigners to apply online using SingPass/MyInfo or in-branch. Required documents for foreigners (not using SingPass): passport biodata page, Employment Pass or notification letter, and proof of residential address (IPA letter from MOM, employment letter, or utility bill). Some banks also accept an IPA letter as proof of address before the physical EP card arrives, making it possible to open an account within the first week of arrival.
required_documents: Employment Pass card or notification letter (or IPA letter)
proof of residential address (IPA letter, employment letter, or utility/telco bill)
rows.where_to_go: DBS: online (digibank) or any DBS branch; OCBC: online or branch; UOB: branch with reference from existing UOB customer recommended; Citibank/HSBC: branch
rows.notes: DBS explicitly accepts IPA issued by MOM as proof of residential address. Foreigners using SingPass/MyInfo can complete online application faster. Reddit expats confirm IPA + passport is sufficient to open accounts immediately after arrival. DBS Multiplier offers higher interest if salary is credited.
rows.source_quote: In-Principle Approval (IPA) issued by Ministry of Manpower

rows.title: Get an EZ-Link / SimplyGo card for public transport
rows.description: The EZ-Link card is Singapore's contactless transport card for use on all MRT trains, LRT, public buses, taxis, and selected retail outlets. It is available at 7-Eleven and Cheers convenience stores for S$10 (including S$5 stored value, so the card itself costs S$5). Cards can also be purchased at SimplyGo Ticket Offices at MRT stations. Top up is available at MRT ticketing kiosks, 7-Eleven, DBS/POSB and OCBC ATMs, and via the SimplyGo app. The card is valid for 5 years from encoding and can store up to S$500. Register the card on the SimplyGo app (linked to SingPass) to block it if lost. Alternatively, contactless bank cards and Apple/Google Pay are accepted on SimplyGo-enabled readers.
rows.where_to_go: 7-Eleven or Cheers convenience stores; SimplyGo Ticket Offices at MRT stations
rows.notes: S$10 purchase price (S$5 card fee + S$5 stored value). SimplyGo EZ-Link cards (Account-Based Ticketing) cannot be topped up at convenience stores — only at kiosks and ATMs. From 29 August 2026, AXS Station top-ups will no longer be available. Contactless payment cards also work on buses/MRT.
rows.source_quote: You can purchase EZ-Link cards (non-SimplyGo) from selected convenience stores, such as 7-Eleven or Cheers, at the prevailing retail cost of $10 (with $5 stored-value).

rows.title: Obtain a Singapore SIM card (prepaid or postpaid)
rows.description: Singapore has four main mobile operators: Singtel, StarHub, M1, and MVNO Circles.Life/giga!. Prepaid SIM cards are available immediately at 7-Eleven and Cheers convenience stores, and at airport arrivals with a valid passport — no EP card required. Postpaid plans require an EP card or notification letter and a Singapore bank account or GIRO setup. Prepaid options start from S$10-15. For a postpaid plan (typically better value for long-term residents), approach any operator retail store or apply online with EP card details. A Singapore mobile number is also needed for SingPass SMS two-factor authentication (before setting up the app).
required_documents: Employment Pass card or notification letter (for postpaid)
rows.where_to_go: Prepaid: 7-Eleven, Cheers, Changi Airport arrival halls; Postpaid: Singtel/StarHub/M1/Circles.Life stores or online
rows.notes: Prepaid: passport only, available immediately at Changi Airport and convenience stores. Postpaid: EP card required; GIRO/credit card for billing. M1 Tourist SIM (S$12, 100GB) widely recommended for new arrivals before committing to a postpaid plan. Singapore mobile number required for SingPass SMS 2FA during initial setup.
rows.source_quote: 100GB for use in Singapore · 3GB roaming data for use in Malaysia, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Macau & Thailand

rows.title: Secure housing: rent private property or HDB flat (with quota check)
rows.description: EP holders may rent private condominiums or landed properties without restriction. Renting an HDB flat is also permitted for EP holders, subject to HDB's Non-Citizen Quota — a cap of 8% at the neighbourhood level and 11% at the block level for non-Malaysian non-citizens. The HDB flat owner must obtain HDB's approval before commencing the tenancy. Foreigners generally cannot purchase HDB flats. Purchasing private residential property is possible but attracts a 60% Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) for foreigners (effective 27 April 2023), making renting the practical choice for most EP holders. Private rentals are arranged through property agents or platforms such as PropertyGuru; typical lease is 12-24 months.
required_documents: Employment Pass card or notification letter
rows.where_to_go: Private rentals: via property agents or PropertyGuru/99.co; HDB rental: HDB approval required from flat owner — check quota at services2.hdb.gov.sg/webapp/BR12AWNCQuota/
rows.notes: HDB non-citizen quota check is free and available online. Foreigners cannot buy HDB flats (new or resale). ABSD of 60% applies to any private residential purchase. Typical EP holder rents: 1-bed condo S$2,500-4,500/month; 2-bed S$3,500-6,000/month depending on location. Lease stamp duty (BSD) applies to agreements exceeding 4 years.
rows.source_quote: The quota is applicable if any tenant renting a flat is a non-Malaysian non-citizen, and is set at 8% at the neighbourhood level and 11% at the block level.

rows.title: Understand CPF: EP holders are exempt; obligations begin on PR approval
rows.description: Central Provident Fund (CPF) is Singapore's mandatory retirement, housing, and healthcare savings scheme for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents only. EP and S Pass holders are fully exempt from CPF contributions — neither the employee nor the employer needs to contribute. This exemption has applied since 1 January 2003. However, if an EP holder subsequently obtains Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) status, CPF contributions become mandatory immediately from the date SPR status is granted. In the first two years of SPR status, contributions are made at graduated (lower) rates before moving to full SC/PR rates. EP holders planning to apply for PR should be aware that CPF obligations will commence on PR grant date.
rows.where_to_go: No action required as EP holder; CPF Board (cpf.gov.sg) for information and when PR is granted
rows.notes: CPF contribution rates range from 12.5% to 37% of monthly wages for SC/PR. On becoming SPR, graduated rates apply for years 1-2 before full rates kick in from year 3. Voluntary CPF contributions by EP holders are not permitted. If you SC/PR colleagues need to check CPF, visit cpf.gov.sg.
rows.source_quote: Some employees are exempted from CPF contributions. They include students who fulfil exemption criteria, foreigners, and employees of the United Nations Organisation

rows.title: Register and file Singapore income tax via IRAS myTax Portal
rows.description: All individuals who receive employment income in Singapore must file income tax annually. EP holders earning income in Singapore are tax-resident if they are physically present or employed in Singapore for 183 days or more in the calendar year; resident rates (progressive, up to 24%) are significantly lower than non-resident rates (flat 15% or 22%). Tax filing for individuals opens 1 March each year. The deadline is 18 April for e-filing via myTax Portal (mytax.iras.gov.sg), accessible via SingPass. There is no longer a separate paper filing deadline — as of YA 2025, the due date for paper Form B1/B/M has been aligned to 18 April. First-time filers will receive a notification from IRAS to file. Employer income is typically pre-filled via the Auto-Inclusion Scheme (AIS) for most EP holders.
required_documents: employment income details (auto-filled by employer under AIS)
rows.where_to_go: Online at mytax.iras.gov.sg (login via SingPass)
rows.notes: Filing season opens 1 March annually; deadline is 18 April (e-filing). If employer is in the Auto-Inclusion Scheme, employment income is pre-filled. First-year EP holders may be treated as non-residents if they arrive late in the calendar year (less than 183 days). Penalties apply for late or non-filing.
rows.source_quote: IRAS reminds all individuals and partnerships who need to file that they must do so by 18 April 2026 and declare all sources of income.

rows.title: Understand Singapore tax residency rules and NOR scheme eligibility
rows.description: An individual is a Singapore tax resident if they are physically present or employed in Singapore for 183 days or more in the calendar year. Tax residents pay progressive rates (from 0% to 24% for YA 2024 and beyond). Non-residents pay a flat 15% on employment income or the resident rate, whichever is higher. The Not Ordinarily Resident (NOR) scheme is available to qualifying EP holders who were non-residents of Singapore for three of the four years immediately preceding the year of assessment, and who: (1) spend at least 90 days outside Singapore for business reasons, and (2) earn Singapore employment income of at least S$160,000. The NOR scheme is granted for five consecutive years and allows pro-ration of Singapore tax on time spent outside Singapore for business.
required_documents: travel records (days outside Singapore for business)
rows.where_to_go: Online at mytax.iras.gov.sg; consult a tax advisor for NOR scheme eligibility
rows.notes: The 183-day threshold is the critical determinant of resident vs non-resident status. NOR scheme: must not be a Singapore Citizen or PR; income threshold S$160,000; 90+ business travel days per year required. NOR scheme applications are assessed automatically during filing. Seek professional tax advice for complex situations.
rows.source_quote: You must have spent at least 90 days outside Singapore for business reasons; and Your total Singapore employment income must be at least $160,000.

rows.title: Arrange health insurance — MediShield Life does not cover EP holders
rows.description: MediShield Life is Singapore's national health insurance scheme but it covers Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents only. EP holders are not enrolled in MediShield Life and must arrange their own health insurance. Most employers of EP holders provide group medical insurance as part of the employment package — confirm with your HR team. If not provided, consider: (1) an Integrated Shield Plan from an insurer such as AIA, Prudential, or Great Eastern (these include MediShield Life for SC/PR but EP holders can purchase similar private hospitalization plans), or (2) an international health insurance plan. EP holders without adequate coverage face out-of-pocket costs for hospitalization at Singapore's private hospitals (typically SGD 1,000-5,000+ per night).
required_documents: employment details for employer group policy
rows.where_to_go: HR/employer for group policy confirmation; AIA, Prudential, Great Eastern, AXA for individual private health plans
rows.notes: MediShield Life: SC and PR only — 'protects all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents against large medical bills'. EP holders must purchase private hospitalization insurance. Integrated Shield Plans (ISP) are designed for SC/PR but similar private plans are available to EP holders. Costs vary widely by plan; expect SGD 150-500/month for comprehensive coverage.
rows.source_quote: MediShield Life is a basic health insurance scheme that protects all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents against large medical bills

rows.title: Apply for Student's Pass for school-age children (if applicable)
rows.description: Children of EP holders who hold a Dependant's Pass (DP) or Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) are not required to obtain a separate Student's Pass to attend school within the validity of their existing pass. However, children who hold only a short-term visit pass, or whose DP/LTVP expires during schooling, must apply for a Student's Pass via ICA eService. For government/government-aided schools: apply at least 2 months (and no more than 3 months) before the course starts, online at ICA eService, with a Registration Acknowledgement Letter from the school. A non-refundable S$45 processing fee applies. Processing time is approximately 1 week. Arrange school admission through MOE (moe.gov.sg/international-students) first, then proceed to ICA for the Student's Pass.
required_documents: child's passport biodata page and birth certificate
child's vaccination records (for children aged 12 and under, from 1 Feb 2019)
rows.where_to_go: Step 1: MOE school application at moe.gov.sg/international-students (school allocation); Step 2: ICA Student's Pass eService at ica.gov.sg/reside/STP/apply
rows.notes: S$45 processing fee (approx EUR 31 at 0.69 SGD/EUR). DP and LTVP holders do not need STP while pass is valid. Local sponsor (SC or PR, aged 21+) required if no SC/PR parent. International school enrollment is handled directly by the school; ICA STP still required for full-time international school students.
rows.source_quote: You will need to apply for a Student's Pass if you are a foreigner who has been offered a placement to pursue full-time studies at a Government, Government-aided or independent school in Singapore.

rows.title: Understand Dependant's Pass (DP) and LTVP for accompanying family
rows.description: EP holders earning at least S$6,000/month may bring their spouse (legally married), unmarried children below 21, and stepchildren on a Dependant's Pass (DP). EP holders with fixed monthly salaries of at least S$6,000 may also apply for a Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) for common-law spouses, unmarried handicapped children above 21, unmarried stepchildren above 21, or parents. DP and LTVP applications are submitted by the employer via EP eService after the EP is approved. Each family pass has a S$105 application fee. DP holders may apply for a Letter of Consent (LOC) from MOM to work in Singapore without needing their own separate work pass.
rows.where_to_go: Employer applies via EP eService at mom.gov.sg; family members collect cards at ICA Building after biometrics appointment
rows.notes: Application fee: S$105 per family pass (approx EUR 69). Minimum qualifying salary for EP holder: S$6,000/month. DP holders do not need a separate Student's Pass while DP is valid. Letter of Consent for DP holders to work: applied by employer via MOM. Apply for family passes after main EP is approved.
rows.source_quote: When collecting the card, you will need to show these documents for identification: Person receiving the card, Required documents. Dependant, Passport

rows.title: Note: GST Vouchers and ComCare not available to EP holders
rows.description: Singapore operates several government welfare schemes but most are restricted to Singapore Citizens, and some to Permanent Residents. GST Vouchers (cash, MediSave top-ups, U-Save utility rebates, and S&CC rebates) are available to Singapore Citizens only. ComCare short-to-medium-term assistance (financial assistance for lower-income families) requires the applicant to be a Singapore Citizen or PR with at least one SC immediate family member. CDC (Community Development Council) Vouchers are for Singapore Citizens only. EP holders and other foreigners are not eligible for any of these schemes. EP holders should ensure they have adequate personal savings, private insurance, and employer benefits in lieu of these safety nets.
rows.where_to_go: Not applicable — schemes not available to EP holders
rows.notes: GST Vouchers: Singapore Citizens aged 21+ only. ComCare: SC/PR only (with SC family member). CDC Vouchers: Singapore Citizens only. EP holders should not rely on government social assistance. This step is informational only — there is nothing to file or apply for.
rows.source_name: Ministry of Social and Family Development Singapore (MSF)
rows.source_quote: The applicant must be a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident (where at least one immediate family member of the same household is a Singapore Citizen).

rows.title: Collect S Pass card (for S Pass holders) and complete employer obligations
rows.description: S Pass holders follow a similar process to EP holders. After the S Pass is approved and the IPA letter is issued, the employer must: (1) purchase medical insurance for each S Pass holder and submit details online via myMOM Portal; (2) arrange for the candidate to register fingerprints and photo at ICA if required by the notification letter; and (3) ensure the S Pass card is delivered to the designated address within 4 working days after registration or document verification. Employers in construction, marine, and process (CMP) sectors must also purchase a Primary Care Plan for S Pass holders. S Pass holders' FIN numbers are printed on their cards and work identically to EP holder FINs for SingPass and other government services.
rows.where_to_go: ICA for biometrics registration (if required by notification letter); card delivered by post to designated address
rows.notes: S Pass minimum salary: S$3,150/month (as of 2025, rising progressively). Employer must submit medical insurance details via myMOM Portal. Card delivery is within 4 working days (vs 5 for EP). CMP sector employers must also enroll S Pass holders in a Primary Care Plan. S Pass holders can register SingPass using their FIN identically to EP holders.
rows.source_quote: Make an appointment for the candidate to register their fingerprints and photo; Buy medical insurance for each pass holder and submit the insurance details online

rows.title: Apply for Social Security Number (SSN)
rows.description: A Social Security Number (SSN) is the foundational US government identifier required for employment, tax filing, banking, credit, and most government services. Noncitizens authorized to work in the US are eligible for an SSN. You must wait at least 10 days after arriving in the US (to allow DHS records to update) before applying — many SSA offices recommend waiting at least 2 weeks. Apply in person at a local SSA office with your original documents. The SSA cannot issue an SSN on the basis of photocopies. The card itself typically arrives 2–4 weeks after approval; allow up to 6 weeks. While waiting for your SSN card, you may present your receipt notice from the SSA to your employer; most employers can start you on payroll using your SSN once verbally confirmed, pending the physical card.
required_documents: Immigration document showing work authorization — Form I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record)
Work authorization: I-797 Approval Notice, Employment Authorization Document (EAD/Form I-766), or H-1B/L-1 visa stamp
If applicable: Form I-20 (F-1 students) or DS-2019 (J-1 exchange visitors)
rows.where_to_go: Local Social Security Administration (SSA) office — find nearest office at https://www.ssa.gov/locator
rows.notes: Cannot apply until at least 10 days after arrival (DHS records sync). Processing for the card takes 2–6 weeks after the application. state_variation_note: Processing times may vary by local SSA office workload. Some state DMVs can submit SSN applications on your behalf during driver's license application (Real ID-compliant states). Do not share your SSN unnecessarily once received — it is the primary identity credential in the US.
rows.source_quote: If you are not a U.S. citizen, we can issue you a Social Security number if you are lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence or under a visa that allows you to work in the United States.

rows.title: Apply for ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) — if not SSN-eligible
rows.description: An ITIN is a 9-digit tax processing number issued by the IRS (beginning with '9') for individuals who are required to have a US taxpayer identification number but are not eligible for a Social Security Number. This applies to: dependents of US citizens or residents who are foreign nationals, nonresident aliens with US tax obligations not tied to employment (e.g., rental income, investments), and spouses of US workers who do not themselves have work authorization. An ITIN does NOT authorize employment, change immigration status, or provide eligibility for Social Security benefits or the Earned Income Tax Credit. File Form W-7 (Application for IRS Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) together with a completed federal tax return (Form 1040 or 1040-NR). Applications can be submitted by mail, in-person at an IRS Taxpayer Assistance Center, or through a Certifying Acceptance Agent (CAA) who can authenticate documents on-site so you do not need to mail original documents.
required_documents: Completed federal tax return (Form 1040 or 1040-NR) — attached to W-7
Passport (original or certified copy) — acceptable as both identity and foreign status proof
OR two supporting documents: one proving identity (e.g., government-issued photo ID), one proving foreign status (e.g., visa documentation)
If claiming treaty benefits: additional treaty documentation
rows.where_to_go: Mail to IRS Austin Service Center, P.O. Box 149342, Austin, TX 78714-9342; OR in-person at an IRS Taxpayer Assistance Center with ITIN services — find at https://www.irs.gov/help/tac-locations-where-in-person-document-review-is-provided; OR via a Certifying Acceptance Agent
rows.notes: Processing time: 'Allow 7 weeks for us to notify you about your ITIN application status.' Extends to 9–11 weeks during tax season (January 15 – April 30) or for overseas applications. You receive CP565 (assigned), CP566 (more info needed), or CP567 (rejected). state_variation_note: ITIN is a federal IRS number — state tax treatment of ITIN holders varies; check your state's revenue department.
rows.source_quote: Allow 7 weeks for us to notify you about your ITIN application status (9 to 11 weeks if you apply during tax season (Jan. 15 – Apr. 30) or if you're filing from overseas).

rows.title: Obtain State Driver's License or State ID (REAL ID compliant)
rows.description: Each US state issues driver's licenses and non-driver state ID cards through its Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or equivalent agency. As of May 7, 2025, the federal REAL ID Act is fully enforced: a REAL ID-compliant card (marked with a gold or black star) is required to board domestic flights and access certain federal facilities. Non-REAL ID licenses are no longer accepted at TSA checkpoints — a valid passport remains an acceptable alternative for air travel. To obtain a REAL ID-compliant license or state ID, you must present: (1) proof of identity (passport or birth certificate), (2) proof of Social Security Number (SSN card, W-2, or pay stub with full SSN), (3) two proofs of state residency (utility bill, bank statement, lease agreement — both must show your name and address), and (4) proof of lawful status (visa, I-94, I-797, EAD). Most states require an in-person visit. Non-SSN holders may be issued a non-REAL ID license in some states with a 'NOT FOR REAL ID PURPOSES' notation. Timing: apply only after establishing a local address. Processing varies by state from same-day to 4–6 weeks for a mailed card.
required_documents: Passport (original) — proof of identity and foreign status
Social Security Number card, or document displaying full SSN (W-2, pay stub)
Two documents proving state residency (utility bill, bank statement, lease agreement — must show current address)
Proof of lawful status: visa stamp, Form I-94, I-797 approval notice, or EAD
If applicable: current out-of-state or foreign driver's license
rows.where_to_go: Your state's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or equivalent. Find your state's DMV at https://www.usa.gov/motor-vehicle-services
rows.notes: REAL ID enforcement began May 7, 2025. A valid US passport can substitute for a REAL ID for air travel. state_variation_note: Required documents, fees, and processing times vary significantly by state. Some states (e.g., California, New York) allow undocumented residents to obtain non-REAL ID licenses under state law. Some states have appointment-only DMV systems — check online before visiting. International driving permits are recognized for short periods (typically 1 year) from arrival.
rows.source_name: US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) — REAL ID
rows.source_quote: Beginning May 7, 2025, every air traveler 18 years of age and older will need a REAL ID-compliant driver's license or another acceptable form of identification to fly within the United States.

rows.title: Open a US Bank Account
rows.description: Opening a US bank account is essential for receiving your salary, paying bills, and building a US financial presence. Most major US banks (Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citibank) will open a checking account for foreign nationals with a valid passport and visa as primary ID, though they typically prefer or require an SSN or ITIN for full account features (e.g., online banking, debit card). Some branches of Citibank, HSBC USA, and Bank of America participate in international customer programs that facilitate pre-arrival or early account opening. If you do not yet have an SSN or ITIN, consider: (1) a bank that accepts an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) plus passport — many credit unions and community banks accept this, (2) digital/fintech banks such as Wise (formerly TransferWise) or Revolut that serve as bridge accounts requiring only passport for identity verification and no SSN, or (3) opening an account at a branch of your home country's bank if it operates in the US. Once you receive your SSN, update your bank records immediately to unlock full account functionality and start building a banking history.
required_documents: US visa or I-94 (proof of lawful status)
SSN or ITIN (if available; some banks accept ITIN in lieu of SSN)
US residential address (utility bill or lease agreement)
rows.where_to_go: Branch of chosen bank; some banks allow online application. Wise and Revolut accounts can be opened fully online at wise.com and revolut.com.
rows.notes: FDIC-insured banks protect deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per institution. Without SSN, some banks will restrict international wire transfers or online features. state_variation_note: Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) and credit unions in major immigrant-destination cities often have streamlined programs for new arrivals — check FDIC BankFind for FDIC-insured local institutions. Fintech bridge accounts (Wise, Revolut) do not count toward US credit history but serve immediate banking needs.
rows.source_quote: The FDIC insures deposits of up to $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, per ownership category.

rows.title: Enroll in Health Insurance
rows.description: The US does not have a universal health insurance system; coverage is primarily obtained through your employer, a government marketplace, or a government program. Most employers offering group health insurance have a new hire enrollment window (typically 30–60 days from your start date) — missing this window means you must wait until the annual Open Enrollment period (typically November 1 – January 15 for ACA marketplace plans). Options: (1) Employer-sponsored insurance (ESI): most common for full-time employees; premiums are deducted pre-tax from payroll. (2) ACA Marketplace (healthcare.gov): for employees whose employer does not offer insurance, or those in the gap before employer insurance starts; moving to the US from abroad triggers a 'Special Enrollment Period' of 60 days. (3) Medicaid/CHIP: for low-income individuals and families; lawfully present immigrants may be eligible after a 5-year waiting period in most states, though several states (CA, NY, WA, others) have eliminated this waiting period for children and pregnant women. (4) COBRA: allows continuation of a previous employer's US health plan for up to 18 months, but at full cost to the employee. If you are on an F, J, or other student/exchange visa, your visa sponsor may require specific insurance coverage.
required_documents: Proof of employer hire date (offer letter or HR confirmation)
SSN or ITIN (for ACA marketplace enrollment)
Proof of immigration status (for Medicaid/CHIP or ACA subsidy eligibility)
rows.where_to_go: Employer HR department for ESI; healthcare.gov for ACA marketplace; your state's Medicaid agency for Medicaid/CHIP
rows.notes: Do not miss the new-hire enrollment window — it is typically 30–60 days and cannot be extended except for qualifying life events. ACA Open Enrollment runs November 1 – January 15 annually. Moving to the US from abroad qualifies as a Special Enrollment Period trigger. state_variation_note: Medicaid eligibility and waiting periods vary significantly by state. Several states (CA, NY, WA, IL, MA, MN) have expanded Medicaid to cover immigrants during the 5-year federal waiting period. Without health insurance in the US, a single hospital visit can cost thousands of dollars.
rows.source_quote: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) gives more people access to health insurance. COBRA insurance lets qualified workers keep their group health insurance for a limited time after a change in eligibility.

rows.title: Complete Federal Tax Withholding Enrollment (Form W-4)
rows.description: On or before your first day of employment, your employer will require you to complete Form W-4 (Employee's Withholding Certificate). This form instructs your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. For US residents and those who will file as resident aliens for tax purposes, standard W-4 completion applies. Nonresident aliens (those who do not pass the Green Card Test or Substantial Presence Test) must follow special IRS rules: they must claim 'Single' or 'Married Filing Separately' status, claim only one standard withholding adjustment, and may not claim 'Exempt' from withholding. Nonresident aliens on F, J, M, or Q visas performing services directly related to their nonimmigrant status are generally exempt from Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes. H-1B, L-1, O-1, and similar work visa holders are subject to full FICA withholding. Your employer will also typically register your state income tax withholding using your state's equivalent withholding form (e.g., CA DE-4, NY IT-2104). Note: 43 states + DC impose a state income tax; Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming do not tax earned income.
required_documents: Completed Form W-4 (IRS) — provided by employer
SSN (required field on W-4 — if not yet received, notify HR and provide once obtained)
State equivalent withholding form (provided by employer)
rows.where_to_go: Employer HR/payroll department; Form W-4 available at https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/fw4.pdf
rows.notes: Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator (https://www.irs.gov/individuals/tax-withholding-estimator) to determine the optimal withholding. Nonresident aliens should also review IRS Publication 519 (US Tax Guide for Aliens). state_variation_note: State withholding forms and requirements differ by state. Some states (TX, FL, NV, WA, etc.) have no state income tax — no state form needed. FICA exemption for F/J/M/Q visa holders requires employer HR to code the exception correctly in payroll systems.
rows.source_quote: Complete Form W-4 so that your employer can withhold the correct federal income tax from your pay.

rows.title: Understand FICA Withholding (Social Security & Medicare Taxes)
rows.description: FICA (Federal Insurance Contributions Act) taxes fund Social Security (6.2% employee share, up to the annual wage base — $168,600 in 2024) and Medicare (1.45% employee share, with an additional 0.9% on wages over $200,000). Employers match these contributions. Whether FICA applies depends on your visa and tax residency status. Most work visa holders (H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E-3, green card holders) are fully subject to FICA withholding. Exempt categories include: (1) F-1, J-1, M-1, and Q visa holders who are nonresident aliens performing services related to the purpose of their admission — exempt from both Social Security and Medicare taxes. (2) A-visa foreign government employees, G-visa international organization employees, and D-visa crew members under certain conditions. (3) H-2A agricultural workers under specific treaty conditions. If your employer incorrectly withholds FICA taxes, you may request a refund via Form 843. The US has Totalization Agreements with 30+ countries to prevent double Social Security taxation — if you are paying into your home country's social security system under a posted worker arrangement, you may be exempt from US FICA.
required_documents: Visa documentation (to verify exempt status if applicable)
Form 843 (if seeking refund of incorrectly withheld FICA taxes)
rows.where_to_go: Employer HR/payroll department; IRS for corrections at https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/aliens-employed-in-the-us-social-security-taxes
rows.notes: H-1B workers are generally subject to full FICA. F-1/J-1 students in their nonresident alien period are exempt. Confirm your exemption status with your employer's payroll/tax department on Day 1. state_variation_note: FICA is a federal tax — no state variation. However, some states have additional disability insurance taxes (e.g., California SDI, New York SDI) that are separate from FICA.
rows.source_name: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — Aliens Employed in the US: Social Security Taxes
rows.source_quote: Nonresident alien students, scholars, professors, teachers, trainees, researchers, and other aliens temporarily present in the United States in F-1, J-1, M-1, or Q-1/Q-2 nonimmigrant status are exempt from Social Security / Medicare taxes.

rows.title: Enroll Children in Public School
rows.description: All children in the US, regardless of immigration status, have the constitutional right to a free public education through grade 12 (established by the Supreme Court in Plyler v. Doe, 457 US 202 (1982)). Public schools are organized by school district — your children will attend the school(s) in the district where you live. Enrollment is handled at the district or school level. Typical required documents: proof of residency in the district (lease, utility bill), proof of the child's age (birth certificate or passport), immunization/vaccination records, and previous school records (transcript, report cards). Schools may not require Social Security Numbers from students or parents, nor may they inquire about immigration status as a condition of enrollment. If you do not yet have a permanent address, the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act guarantees school enrollment before a permanent address is established — contact the school district's homeless/migrant liaison. Vaccinations: states differ in required immunizations (commonly: MMR, DTaP, varicella, Hep B, polio, Tdap); most offer medical and religious exemptions. Records from foreign countries may need to be translated and may require a catch-up vaccination schedule.
required_documents: Proof of residency in the school district (lease agreement, utility bill, or employer letter)
Child's birth certificate or passport (proof of age)
Immunization/vaccination records (translated if in a foreign language)
Previous school records and transcripts (helpful but not mandatory)
rows.where_to_go: Your local public school district enrollment office — find your district via the National Center for Education Statistics school locator at https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/schoolsearch/ or your district's website
rows.notes: Schools cannot deny enrollment based on immigration status. SSN is NOT required for school enrollment. state_variation_note: Vaccination schedules required for school enrollment vary significantly by state — check your state's health department website. Some states (e.g., California) have eliminated non-medical exemptions for vaccinations. Districts in high-immigrant-population areas (NYC, LA, Chicago, Houston) often have multilingual enrollment staff and immigrant family support programs.
rows.source_quote: Under Plyler v. Doe, all children, regardless of their immigration status, have the right to a free public education through high school.

rows.title: Get a US SIM Card / Mobile Phone Plan
rows.description: Activating a US phone number is one of the most immediately practical steps upon arrival — it is required for two-factor authentication, bank account setup, and general communications. Two main options: (1) Prepaid SIM plans: require no SSN, no credit check, and minimal ID. Available immediately at carrier stores, airport kiosks, and retail outlets (Walmart, Best Buy, CVS). Major prepaid carriers include T-Mobile Prepaid, AT&T Prepaid, Mint Mobile (T-Mobile network), Boost Mobile, and Straight Talk. Plans typically start at $15–$45/month for unlimited talk/text and 5–15GB data. (2) Postpaid (contract) plans: offered by T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, etc.; typically require SSN for a credit check and may require a deposit of $100–$250 from those with no US credit history. If you have an unlocked international phone, purchasing a prepaid SIM upon arrival is the fastest path. eSIM options (Airalo, T-Mobile eSIM) can be activated digitally before arrival. Most carriers do not require a US ID for prepaid — a foreign passport is typically sufficient.
required_documents: For prepaid: passport or any photo ID (many carriers require no ID at all for cash prepaid)
For postpaid: SSN or ITIN, government-issued ID, and possibly a deposit if no US credit history
rows.where_to_go: Carrier retail stores (T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon), Walmart/Target electronics sections, or order eSIM online at mint.com, airalo.com, or carrier websites
rows.notes: Prepaid SIM is the fastest option on or before Day 1 — no SSN required. eSIM activation is possible before leaving your home country for select carriers. state_variation_note: Coverage quality varies significantly by region — T-Mobile has best rural coverage in some areas; Verizon is strongest on the East Coast. Consider checking coverage maps before choosing a carrier. Number portability: you can keep your US number when switching carriers.
rows.source_quote: Prepaid plans often don't require a credit check or long-term contract.

rows.title: Set Up Utilities (Electricity, Gas, Internet)
rows.description: Once you have a residential address, you will need to establish utility services. The US utility market is largely privatized and varies by city and state. Electricity and natural gas are typically provided by regulated monopoly utilities (e.g., Con Edison in NYC, Pacific Gas & Electric in Northern California, ComEd in Chicago). Internet/broadband is provided competitively in most urban areas (Comcast/Xfinity, Charter/Spectrum, AT&T, Verizon Fios). Steps: (1) Contact your landlord to confirm which utilities are separately metered (many apartments include water; some include gas); (2) Contact the local utility company by phone or their website to establish service in your name; (3) Expect a security deposit of $100–$300 if you have no US credit history — this deposit is typically refunded after 12 months of on-time payment; (4) Internet setup typically requires scheduling an installation visit (allow 1–2 weeks) or self-installation with a provided kit. For internet, T-Mobile and Verizon offer home internet with no credit check and no installation visit. National grid and utility provider information is available through your local municipality website. Google 'electric utility [your city]' to find your provider.
required_documents: Lease agreement or proof of residence
SSN or ITIN (preferred by utilities for credit check; deposit may substitute)
Payment method (bank account or credit/debit card for automatic billing)
rows.where_to_go: Utility company websites or phone lines; find local utilities at https://www.electricchoice.com/map-of-electricity-deregulation/ (for deregulated states) or your municipality's website
rows.notes: Deposits are common for new arrivals without US credit history. Deposit amounts range from $100–$300 and are typically refunded after 12 months. state_variation_note: 24 states have deregulated electricity markets where you can choose your electricity supplier (Texas, Ohio, Illinois, NY, NJ, PA, etc.) — this can mean significant cost savings but requires comparing offers. In regulated states, one monopoly utility serves each area. Natural gas is not available in all areas — electric-only residences are common in newer buildings.
rows.source_quote: You can save energy and money in your home by being informed about your utility options.

rows.title: Start Building US Credit History
rows.description: The US uses a credit scoring system (FICO score, range 300–850; VantageScore as alternative) maintained by three major credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Foreign credit history is not automatically recognized in the US — you start as 'credit invisible' with no US credit file. This affects your ability to rent an apartment, finance a car, get a credit card, or eventually obtain a mortgage. The fastest legitimate strategies to build credit from zero: (1) Secured credit card: You deposit money (typically $200–$500) as collateral, and the card issuer grants you a credit line equal to the deposit. Use it for small purchases and pay the full balance monthly. The card reports your payment history to credit bureaus, building your score. Look for cards with no annual fee (Discover it Secured, Capital One Secured are well-regarded). (2) Become an authorized user on a trusted person's existing credit card account. (3) Credit-builder loan from a credit union or community bank — your payments are reported to bureaus. (4) Nova Credit Credit Passport: For citizens of 26+ countries including UK, Canada, Australia, India, Mexico, and others — Nova Credit can import your foreign credit history and translate it into a US-equivalent report accepted by American Express, MPOWER Financing, and select other lenders. (5) Some banks offer credit cards to new arrivals with passport + visa even without SSN (Citibank Global Credit Transfer, HSBC Expat).
required_documents: SSN or ITIN (for secured credit card applications at most US banks)
Passport + visa (for passport-only credit card programs)
rows.where_to_go: Bank or credit union branch; secured cards available at Discover (discover.com), Capital One (capitalone.com), and many banks; Nova Credit at novacredit.com; free annual credit report at annualcreditreport.com
rows.notes: Credit scores are used for apartment rentals, car insurance, phone contracts (postpaid), and loans. Aim to keep credit utilization below 30% and always pay on time. state_variation_note: No state variation in federal credit reporting laws. CFPB research found 26 million Americans are 'credit invisible' — a common challenge for new arrivals.
rows.source_quote: There are 26 million consumers who are credit invisible — who don't have sufficient credit history with the major credit reporting companies.

rows.title: Register a Motor Vehicle and Obtain Auto Insurance
rows.description: If you bring a vehicle from abroad or purchase one in the US, you must register it with your state's DMV and obtain state-minimum auto insurance before driving. Vehicle registration is done at the state level. For vehicles brought from abroad: US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) must clear the vehicle (EPA and DOT compliance required), and a 25-year-old vehicle exemption applies to classic cars. For vehicles purchased in the US: the dealership typically handles initial registration paperwork, though title transfer to your name requires DMV processing. Auto insurance is mandatory in 49 states (New Hampshire is the exception, though financial responsibility is still required). Minimum coverage requirements vary by state (e.g., 25/50/25 in California means $25K/$50K bodily injury, $25K property damage). As a new arrival with no US driving history, expect higher premiums — international driving records may be considered by some insurers. Progressive, GEICO, and State Farm are major national insurers who may recognize foreign driving history. An international driving permit (IDP) issued by your home country's automobile association is generally accepted for the first year.
required_documents: Valid state driver's license (REAL ID or standard)
Proof of auto insurance (required before registration in most states)
Payment for registration fees (typically $50–$300 depending on state and vehicle value)
If imported: CBP Form 7501 (Entry Summary) and EPA/DOT compliance documentation
rows.where_to_go: Your state's DMV — find at https://www.usa.gov/motor-vehicle-services
rows.notes: Auto insurance is legally required before driving in most states. As a new arrival with no US credit or insurance history, deposits and higher premiums are common. state_variation_note: Registration fees, renewal schedules, emissions inspection requirements, and minimum insurance coverage requirements vary significantly by state. Some states (CA, NY, NJ) have higher minimum coverage requirements. Texas and Florida have no-fault insurance requirements. Vehicles must be registered in the state where you primarily reside.
rows.source_quote: Each state has its own requirements for vehicle registration. Contact your state's motor vehicle agency to find out the requirements in your state.

rows.title: Set Up US Postal Address and Mail Services
rows.description: Establishing a reliable US mailing address is essential for receiving government correspondence, financial statements, and packages. Options: (1) Residential address: simply receive mail at your home address — no setup required other than notifying senders. Notify all important contacts (bank, SSA, IRS, employer) of your US address promptly. (2) USPS PO Box: rent a dedicated mailbox at your local Post Office. Available in 5 sizes, rental periods of 3, 6, or 12 months. Reserve online at usps.com and complete the setup in-person with 2 forms of valid US ID within 30 days. Costs: ~$15–$265/year depending on size and location. (3) USPS Mail Forwarding from your previous address: if you have a prior US address or need mail forwarded from abroad (limited to US domestic forwarding), submit a Change of Address form (PS Form 3575) online for $1.25 identity verification fee or in-person at any Post Office for free. First-Class mail and periodicals forward at no extra cost. Marketing Mail does not forward. (4) Private mailbox services (UPS Store, PostalAnnex) offer a street address (not a PO Box number), which can be used as a business address. Important: notify US government agencies (SSA, IRS, USCIS) of address changes separately — USPS change of address does NOT update government records automatically.
required_documents: For PO Box: 2 forms of valid US ID (passport + any secondary ID; secondary can be utility bill or bank statement)
For mail forwarding: online ($1.25 fee + mobile verification) or in-person (photo ID)
rows.where_to_go: USPS online at usps.com or any US Post Office — find locations at tools.usps.com/find-location.htm
rows.notes: PO Box application must be completed in-person within 30 days of online reservation to receive keys. First-Class mail forwarding is free and lasts 12 months (extendable for additional fee). state_variation_note: PO Box pricing varies by ZIP code and local postal volume — metropolitan areas (NYC, LA, SF) tend to have higher prices and waiting lists for convenient sizes. USPS premium mail forwarding services can also pack and ship mail weekly/daily.
rows.source_quote: Visit the Post Office within 30 days with 2 forms of acceptable U.S. identification to receive your keys or combination.

rows.title: Understand Annual Federal and State Tax Filing Obligations
rows.description: All individuals who earn income in the US must file annual tax returns. The federal tax year runs January 1 – December 31; returns are due April 15 of the following year (or next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday). Federal filing: residents and resident aliens file Form 1040; nonresident aliens file Form 1040-NR. Nonresident aliens cannot claim the standard deduction (with narrow exceptions) and are taxed only on US-source income. Resident aliens (those who pass the Green Card Test or Substantial Presence Test) are taxed on worldwide income, same as US citizens. Your tax residency status is separate from your immigration status — you may be a nonresident for immigration purposes but a resident for tax purposes if you have been in the US long enough. State income tax returns are filed separately in the 41 states + DC that impose state income tax, typically due on April 15 as well. Tax preparation resources: the IRS Free File program offers free federal filing for individuals earning under $79,000 (2024 threshold). IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) sites provide free in-person tax help. Nonresident aliens cannot use some commercial tax software — specialized software (Sprintax, Glacier) is designed for nonresident alien returns.
required_documents: Form W-2 (wage statement from employer — issued by January 31)
Form 1042-S (if applicable — for income subject to withholding under tax treaty)
Form 1095-A if enrolled in ACA marketplace health insurance
rows.where_to_go: IRS Free File at freefile.irs.gov; VITA sites at irs.gov/vita; nonresident alien tax software: Sprintax at sprintax.com or Glacier at online-tax.net
rows.notes: Nonresident aliens must file Form 1040-NR, not the standard 1040. Departure from the US requires a 'sailing permit' / tax clearance (Form 1040-C or 2063) before leaving. state_variation_note: 9 states have no state income tax (AK, FL, NV, NH, SD, TN, TX, WA, WY). 41 states + DC require separate state returns. State filing deadlines are usually April 15 but confirm with your state's revenue department.
rows.source_name: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — Taxation of Nonresident Aliens
rows.source_quote: A nonresident alien is an alien who has not passed the green card test or the substantial presence test. If you are a nonresident alien at the end of the tax year, you must file Form 1040-NR.

rows.title: Understand Medicaid and Medicare Eligibility
rows.description: Medicaid is a joint federal-state program providing health coverage for low-income individuals. Medicare is the federal health insurance program for people aged 65+ and certain disabled individuals. For newly arrived employees who are working age and employed, these programs are less likely to be immediately relevant, but knowing eligibility rules is important for dependents and planning. Medicaid for immigrants: most lawfully present immigrants are subject to a 5-year waiting period (5-year bar) before becoming eligible for federal Medicaid. However, many states (CA, NY, WA, IL, MA, MN, OR, CT, ME, VT) have used state funds to eliminate or shorten this waiting period, especially for children and pregnant women. Children of immigrants may be eligible for CHIP (Children's Health Insurance Program) regardless of parents' immigration status in several states. Medicare: available to individuals aged 65+ who have paid Social Security taxes for at least 10 years (40 quarters), or to certain disabled individuals. New arrivals typically do not qualify for Medicare until they have lived and worked in the US for at least 10 years. Emergency Medicaid: available to lawfully present immigrants for emergency medical conditions only, regardless of the 5-year bar.
required_documents: Proof of income and household size
Proof of immigration status (for Medicaid eligibility determination)
rows.where_to_go: Your state's Medicaid agency — apply via healthcare.gov which routes to state agencies; Medicare information at medicare.gov
rows.notes: Most new working-age arrivals will use employer-sponsored insurance rather than Medicaid. state_variation_note: Medicaid eligibility and the 5-year immigrant bar are subject to significant state-level variation. As of 2024, at least 14 states have eliminated or reduced the 5-year waiting period for at least some immigrant populations. Always check your state's current Medicaid rules as they change frequently.
rows.source_quote: Medicaid provides benefits to adults with a low income, children, pregnant women, people age 65 or over, and people with disabilities. Each state has its own requirements.

rows.title: Determine Tax Residency Status (Resident vs Nonresident Alien)
rows.description: Your US tax residency status determines which tax form you file and how broadly you are taxed. This is distinct from your immigration status. The IRS uses two tests: (1) Green Card Test: if you are a lawful permanent resident (green card holder) at any time during the year, you are a resident alien for tax purposes. (2) Substantial Presence Test (SPT): you are a resident alien if you are physically present in the US for 183 days or more, calculated as: all days in the current year + 1/3 of days in the prior year + 1/6 of days two years ago. F-1, J-1, M-1, Q-1 visa holders in 'exempt individual' status do not count days for SPT purposes (F-1 for 5 calendar years; J-1/Q-1 for 2 calendar years in some cases). Resident aliens are taxed on worldwide income (same as US citizens). Nonresident aliens are taxed only on US-source income. If you change status during the year (from nonresident to resident), you may be a 'dual status alien' and must file a special return. Many tax treaties between the US and other countries provide reduced tax rates or exemptions on certain types of income — claim treaty benefits on Form 8833 or on Form 1040-NR.
required_documents: US entry dates and I-94 history (available at i94.cbp.dhs.gov)
rows.where_to_go: IRS at irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/determination-of-tax-residency-status; employer HR/tax department; or international tax professional
rows.notes: Misclassifying your tax residency status is one of the most common errors for newly arrived foreign nationals. H-1B workers typically become resident aliens for tax purposes after passing the Substantial Presence Test. F-1 and J-1 students are exempt individuals for SPT purposes for 5 and 2 calendar years respectively. state_variation_note: Tax residency determination is federal — however, state tax residency rules (which affect state filing obligations) are set independently by each state and may differ from federal rules.
rows.source_quote: A nonresident alien is an alien who has not passed the green card test or the substantial presence test.

rows.title: Set Up Mail Forwarding from Previous Country
rows.description: USPS domestic mail forwarding is available for mail within the US only — it does NOT forward mail from a foreign country. For international mail redirection, you must separately arrange forwarding with your home country's postal service or a private virtual mailbox service. Options: (1) In the US: if you had a prior US address, file a USPS Change of Address (Form PS 3575) online ($1.25) or in-person (free). Standard forwarding: First-Class mail and periodicals forward at no extra cost for 12 months; Marketing Mail does not forward; packages forward free. Allow 2 weeks for forwarding to activate. (2) From abroad: contract with a virtual mailbox provider in your home country (e.g., UK Royal Mail Keepsafe, or a private service like PostScan Mail) to scan and forward important mail to your US address. (3) Notify all critical senders directly of your new US address: IRS, SSA, USCIS, your home country's tax authority, banks, insurers, and professional registrations. Change of address with USPS does not automatically notify any government agency.
required_documents: For USPS online change: mobile phone for identity verification
For in-person USPS: valid photo ID
rows.where_to_go: USPS Change of Address at moversguide.usps.com; or any US Post Office for in-person submission
rows.notes: USPS forwarding applies only to US domestic mail. state_variation_note: No state variation — USPS is a federal service. Beware of unofficial 'change of address' websites that charge higher fees — the official USPS process is $1.25 online (identity verification fee) or free in-person.
rows.source_name: United States Postal Service (USPS) — Mail Forwarding
rows.source_quote: Your change of address order only changes your mailing address with the Post Office. You will still need to contact any important agencies, businesses, or services to update your address.

rows.title: Understand COBRA Continuation Coverage
rows.description: COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) allows employees and their families to continue group health insurance coverage from a former employer for a limited period after leaving a job, losing coverage, or experiencing certain qualifying life events. COBRA is relevant for employees who: had US employer-sponsored health insurance previously, are between jobs, or experienced a reduction in hours making them ineligible for employer coverage. COBRA coverage typically lasts 18 months (36 months for certain qualifying events). The key limitation: under COBRA, you pay the full premium (both employee and employer shares) plus up to 2% administrative fee — costs can be $500–$2,000+/month for a family. You have 60 days from the qualifying event to elect COBRA coverage; coverage is retroactive to the date of the triggering event. For new arrivals who have not previously had US employer coverage, COBRA is generally not applicable — the ACA marketplace or employer enrollment windows are the relevant options.
